readerTitle: A forecast is a prediction, not a wish
caseNote: 가상 사례 (대기업 안의 지역 영업팀, 배관 업체, 청소 업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 예측은 '원하는 숫자'가 아니라 '실제로 일어날 것 같은 숫자'다. 목표와 분리해야 문제를 일찍 보여주는 경보 장치로 쓸 수 있다.
misconception: 예측은 목표를 다르게 부르는 말이다. 예측을 낮게 잡으면 의지가 약한 것이다.

sources.text: 관리회계·재무계획의 표준 개념 (예측과 예산·목표의 구분, 동인 기반 예측)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 배관 업체 계산: 주당 문의 40건 × 예약 전환 60% = 24건 × 평균 작업 $250 = 주당 $6,000. 다시 확인 필요.
영업팀 사례의 목표 $2M과 가중 파이프라인 $1.7M은 가상 수치입니다. '가중 파이프라인(성사 확률을 곱한 진행 중 거래 합계)'이라는 설명이 독자에게 충분히 쉬운지 검토하세요.

cards.title: A forecast is a prediction, not a wish
body: The weather app says 70% chance of rain on Saturday. You planned a picnic. The forecaster doesn't care, and that's exactly why the forecast is useful.
Business forecasts often work the other way. They say what the plan needs, not what is likely. And the bad news arrives late.

image.label: Picnic blanket under a phone showing a rain forecast
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 잔디 위에 피크닉 바구니와 담요, 그 위에 떠 있는 스마트폰 화면에 비구름 아이콘과 "70%". 하늘 한쪽에 먹구름이 다가옴. 실제 날씨 앱 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Finance wants your number.
body: You lead a regional sales team inside a larger company. Your target this quarter is $2 million.
You add up the deals in progress, each weighted by how likely it is to close. You get about $1.7 million. Finance asks for your forecast. What do you send?

options.text: $2 million. It's the target, and the team will push to hit it
options.feedback: It shows commitment, but it hides a $300,000 gap from the people who could help close it or plan around it.

options.text: $1.7 million, plus what it would take to close the gap
options.feedback: It's an uncomfortable conversation now. In return, everyone gets ten weeks to react instead of two.

options.text: $1.5 million, so you're sure to beat it
options.feedback: You'll look good at quarter end. But others will under-plan stock and staff, and your forecasts will stop being trusted.

cards.title: Your forecast feeds other people's plans.
body: Say you send $2 million. Finance uses it to approve two new hires. Operations orders stock for $2 million of sales.
By week 10, the gap is obvious. The hires are made and the stock has arrived. Nobody can adjust in time.
Had you sent $1.7 million in week 1, the company could have slowed spending, shifted help to your team, or chased other deals.

image.label: One number flowing into hiring, stock and spending plans
image.brief: 가운데 "Forecast $2.0M" 카드에서 화살표 세 개가 "Hiring", "Stock orders", "Spending" 상자로 이어짐. 오른쪽 타임라인의 10주 차에 "Actual $1.7M" 빨간 표시가 늦게 나타남.

cards.title: Forecast
body: A **forecast** is your best honest estimate of what will actually happen, based on what you know today.
A budget or target answers a different question. It says what you plan to spend or aim to achieve. One asks *what do we want?* The other asks *what do we expect?*
The weather forecaster doesn't predict sunshine because a picnic is planned. A business forecast should work the same way.

cards.title: Build it from what drives the result.
body: Don't start from last year's total plus a hopeful guess. Start from the few things that produce the number. A plumbing business might use:
list: **Share that become booked jobs:** 60%, so 24 jobs
cards.callout: When the forecast moves, you can see which assumption moved.
cards.softwareNote: A subscription business might forecast revenue as current customers × the share who renew, plus expected new sign-ups. If renewals slip, the forecast shows it before the monthly total does.

cards.title: A forecast is supposed to change.
body: The weather forecast for Saturday changes every day as the week goes on. A business forecast should too. New calls, cancellations and signed deals all update it.
Each update shows the gap between what you expect and what you want, while there's still time to act.
One warning sign: if a team's forecast always lands right on its target, it's probably a target dressed up as a forecast.

image.label: Forecast line moving week by week toward the actual result
image.brief: 주 단위 그래프. 점선 "Target"은 위에 평평하게, 실선 "Forecast"는 1주 차부터 매주 조금씩 수정되며 아래쪽 "Actual"에 가까워짐. 초반부터 목표와의 간격이 보이도록 강조.

cards.title: Honest forecasts need a safe place to land.
body: Every forecast is wrong. What matters is by how much, and how early you notice. A single number also hides a range of outcomes.
Honesty depends on how people are treated. Punish low forecasts, and people inflate them. Punish misses, and people pad them low.
Judge forecasts on how accurate they turned out, separately from whether the target was hit.

cards.title: Now it's a cleaning company.
body: You run a house-cleaning business with six cleaners. You'd like to grow 30% this spring and are deciding whether to hire two more.
You have 90 regular clients. New inquiries are running a little below last spring. Which number should drive the hiring decision?

options.text: Plan on 30% growth. That's the goal, and hiring ahead shows you mean it
options.feedback: It keeps ambition high, but if bookings fall short you're paying two cleaners with too little work.

options.text: Forecast from regular clients, current inquiries and how many inquiries usually book
options.feedback: It takes a bit more work, but the hire matches likely demand. If inquiries pick up, you'll see it and can hire then.

options.text: Use last spring's growth, since spring patterns repeat
options.feedback: A sensible starting point. But it ignores the one thing you already know: inquiries are running below last year.

cards.title: Keep what you expect separate from what you want.
body: A target pushes people. A forecast warns them. Mix the two and you lose the warning.
**Try it today:** pick one number you plan around, like monthly sales or bookings. Write your target and your honest expectation side by side. Note the gap.
